extracted.intended_audience: readers of Notes and Queries: literary men, antiquaries, genealogists, historians, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical plan and guidance for antiquarian transcription and cataloguing of church and churchyard inscriptions (who to copy, what to copy, and how to arrange and index the material for use by libraries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and copying of church inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy in full every inscription of an earlier date than 1750; also copy all more modern ones which are in any way remarkable as relating to distinguished persons or containing any peculiarity worthy of note. Reduce the remainder into a tabular form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange the inscriptions of each church chronologically and form an alphabetical index to each inscription in the hundred. Aim to accumulate a mass of valuable matter suitable for reference in a national library; coordinate with other local workers so that a copy of every inscription in every church in England might be prepared. Contact others undertaking the same task so plans may be in unison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and customs for Welsh wedding 'biddings'
rubrics_metrics.description: When a 'bidding' is made in Wales, a printed bidding-letter form is commonly used (printers keep the form in type); the custom is widespread among servants, mechanics, and rural farmers. Gifts given at a bidding are expected to be returned on a similar occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary practice: large procession to church and to the bidding-house (accompanying considered additional obligation); in some towns tea parties now replace biddings (attendees pay and so incur no obligation). Sample bidding-letter structure is provided in full in the issue (listing the young couple and families and requesting the return of gifts when called for). Printers adapt the standard form as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing poetry from autograph manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where autograph manuscript readings differ materially from printed editions, editors/readers should prefer and restore original autograph readings when the variations are of importance to meaning or interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare printed editions with the author's autograph (example given: Coleridge's lines in 'Religious Musings' differ significantly between Pickering's 1844 edition and Coleridge's autograph fragment). When autograph variants affect sense or poetic phrasing, note and, where appropriate, restore the original text and inform readers of the differences.
